title: Single-Row Functions: String & Numeric Narration Scripts

lecture.New_Day7Part1audio01.mp3: Welcome to Day 7! Today, we explore single-row, or scalar functions. Unlike aggregate functions that condense multiple rows into one summary value, single-row functions operate on individual values row by row, returning exactly one transformed output per row.
lecture.New_Day7Part1audio02.mp3: Single-row functions can appear anywhere in your SQL statement: inside the SELECT clause to format data, in the WHERE clause to filter transformed values, in ORDER BY to sort by computed fields, and even in GROUP BY buckets.
lecture.New_Day7Part1audio03.mp3: Let's begin with essential string functions: UPPER and LOWER alter letter casing, LENGTH measures character counts, and TRIM removes surrounding whitespace.
lecture.New_Day7Part1audio04.mp3: In Query 1, we combine first and last name using the standard pipe concatenation operator, convert the email address to uppercase, compute the length of first name, and use REPLACE to strip out the domain name from the email.
lecture.New_Day7Part1audio05.mp3: In Query 2, we use string functions in the WHERE clause: we filter for employees whose cleansed email username has a length of less than 10 characters.
lecture.New_Day7Part1audio06.mp3: Next is SUBSTR, which extracts substrings using a starting position and an optional length. Crucially, SQL indexing is 1-based, not zero-based like Python or JavaScript! Starting at index 1 selects the very first character.
lecture.New_Day7Part1audio07.mp3: In Query 1, SUBSTR extracts a 3-letter abbreviation from the first name. In Query 2, SUBSTR parses text-based hire dates to isolate the 4-digit year and 2-digit month.
lecture.New_Day7Part1audio08.mp3: In Query 3, we pair SUBSTR with INSTR. INSTR locates the character index of the at symbol, and SUBSTR dynamically slices everything after it to isolate the email domain name.
lecture.New_Day7Part1audio09.mp3: Now let's examine numeric functions: ROUND rounds numbers to specified decimal places, CEIL rounds upwards to the nearest integer, FLOOR rounds downwards, and ABS calculates the absolute value.
lecture.New_Day7Part1audio10.mp3: In the numeric demonstration query, we round salary to the nearest thousand using negative decimals, compute estimated monthly pay rounded to 2 decimal places, and calculate absolute deviation from the baseline salary of 70000.
lecture.New_Day7Part1audio11.mp3: Modulo arithmetic calculates the remainder of integer division. In standard SQLite, we use the percent sign operator or the MOD function. Modulo is frequently used to determine odd and even records or partition data across worker batches.
lecture.New_Day7Part1audio12.mp3: For instance, employee ID percent 2 equals zero filters exclusively for even ID numbers, while percent 2 equals 1 targets odd ID numbers.
lecture.New_Day7Part1audio13.mp3: Watch out for NULL handling: any scalar function that receives a NULL argument immediately returns NULL. For example, LENGTH of NULL evaluates to NULL, not zero.
lecture.New_Day7Part1audio14.mp3: Here is an important performance tip: Avoid applying scalar functions directly onto indexed columns in your WHERE clause, as this prevents the query planner from using range index scans. Prefer filtering against raw column boundaries whenever possible.
lecture.New_Day7Part1audio15.mp3: Cross-database comparison: SQLite uses double pipe for string concatenation, PostgreSQL supports both double pipe and CONCAT, and MySQL relies on the CONCAT function.
lecture.New_Day7Part1audio16.mp3: Now that you understand scalar transformations, let's step into the practice arena to master string parsing, mathematical formatting, and cleaning real-world enterprise datasets!

questions.New_Day7Question01.mp3: Generate full employee names! Concatenate first name and last name separated by a space into full name, along with employee ID, from the employees table.
questions.New_Day7Question01sol.mp3: Let's concatenate the names. SELECT employee ID, first name double pipe space double pipe last name as full name... FROM employees.
questions.New_Day7Question02.mp3: Standardize email casing! Return employee ID, first name, and their email address converted to uppercase as upper email from employees.
questions.New_Day7Question02sol.mp3: Let's uppercase the email address. SELECT employee ID, first name, UPPER of email as upper email... FROM employees.
questions.New_Day7Question03.mp3: Extract usernames! From the employees table, return first name, email, and email with the at manodemy dot com domain stripped out using REPLACE, aliased as username.
questions.New_Day7Question03sol.mp3: Let's strip the domain. SELECT first name, email, REPLACE of email comma at manodemy dot com comma empty string as username... FROM employees.
questions.New_Day7Question04.mp3: Measure character lengths! Return first name and the character length of first name as name length from employees, sorted by name length descending.
questions.New_Day7Question04sol.mp3: Let's measure string lengths. SELECT first name, LENGTH of first name as name length... FROM employees... ORDER BY name length DESC.
questions.New_Day7Question05.mp3: Format catalog pricing! Return product ID, product name, and unit price rounded to 1 decimal place as rounded price from the products table.
questions.New_Day7Question05sol.mp3: Let's round the price. SELECT product ID, product name, ROUND of unit price comma 1 as rounded price... FROM products.
questions.New_Day7Question06.mp3: Create 3-letter name abbreviations! Return employee ID, first name, and the first 3 characters of first name using SUBSTR as name code from employees.
questions.New_Day7Question06sol.mp3: Let's extract the prefix. SELECT employee ID, first name, SUBSTR of first name comma 1 comma 3 as name code... FROM employees.
questions.New_Day7Question07.mp3: Calculate estimated monthly compensation! From employees, return first name, salary, and salary divided by 12 rounded to 2 decimal places as monthly salary.
questions.New_Day7Question07sol.mp3: Let's calculate monthly pay. SELECT first name, salary, ROUND of salary divided by 12 point zero comma 2 as monthly salary... FROM employees.
questions.New_Day7Question08.mp3: Calculate salary variance! Return first name, salary, and the absolute difference between salary and 70000 using ABS as salary variance from employees.
questions.New_Day7Question08sol.mp3: Let's compute the absolute difference. SELECT first name, salary, ABS of salary minus 70000 as salary variance... FROM employees.
questions.New_Day7Question09.mp3: Dynamic email domain extraction! Using SUBSTR and INSTR, extract everything after the at symbol in customer emails as email domain, returning customer ID and email domain.
questions.New_Day7Question09sol.mp3: Let's parse the domain dynamically. SELECT customer ID, SUBSTR of email comma INSTR of email comma at symbol plus 1 as email domain... FROM customers.
questions.New_Day7Question10.mp3: Split records by odd and even IDs! Return order ID, customer ID, and total amount for all orders with an even order ID using the modulo operator.
questions.New_Day7Question10sol.mp3: Let's filter for even order IDs. SELECT order ID, customer ID, total amount... FROM orders... WHERE order ID percent 2 equals 0.
questions.New_Day7Question11.mp3: Filter by string length! Find all employees whose last name has 6 or more characters. Return first name, last name, and the length of last name.
questions.New_Day7Question11sol.mp3: Let's filter on string length. SELECT first name, last name, LENGTH of last name as last name length... FROM employees... WHERE LENGTH of last name is greater than or equal to 6.
questions.New_Day7Question12.mp3: Clean customer city names! Return customer ID, city, and city with all leading and trailing whitespace removed using TRIM as clean city from customers.
questions.New_Day7Question12sol.mp3: Let's trim surrounding spaces. SELECT customer ID, city, TRIM of city as clean city... FROM customers.
questions.New_Day7Question13.mp3: Calculate shipping package tiers! For products with a unit price greater than 500, return product name, unit price, and CEIL of unit price divided by 100 as package rating.
questions.New_Day7Question13sol.mp3: Let's apply ceiling division. SELECT product name, unit price, CEIL of unit price divided by 100 point zero as package rating... FROM products... WHERE unit price is greater than 500.
questions.New_Day7Question14.mp3: Create a masked email display! Return customer ID, email, and a masked string showing the first 2 letters followed by three asterisks and the domain using SUBSTR and concatenation.
questions.New_Day7Question14sol.mp3: Let's build the masked email. SELECT customer ID, email, SUBSTR of email comma 1 comma 2 double pipe three asterisks double pipe SUBSTR of email comma INSTR of email comma at symbol as masked email... FROM customers.
questions.New_Day7Question15.mp3: Complex text and numeric formatting! Return product name in lowercase as lower name, unit price, and FLOOR of unit price as floor price for products in category 1, ordered by floor price descending.
questions.New_Day7Question15sol.mp3: Let's combine text and numeric functions. SELECT LOWER of product name as lower name, unit price, FLOOR of unit price as floor price... FROM products... WHERE category ID equals 1... ORDER BY floor price DESC.
